questions.q: Write down the exact formulas for sin(x+y), cos(x+y), and tan(x+y) with all conditions on x and y for which each formula is valid.
questions.a: sin(x+y) = sin x cos y + cos x sin y (valid for all real x, y). cos(x+y) = cos x cos y - sin x sin y (valid for all real x, y). tan(x+y) = (tan x + tan y)/(1 - tan x tan y), valid when x, y, and x+y are not odd multiples of π/2 (i.e., cos x ≠ 0, cos y ≠ 0, cos(x+y) ≠ 0). A wrong answer reveals the student has memorised formulas without understanding domain restrictions—critical for avoiding division by zero in board exams. For example, writing tan(π/2 + π/4) using the formula would be invalid since tan(π/2) is undefined.

questions.q: Explain why sin(x+y) ≠ sin x + sin y by giving a specific counterexample with numerical values, and identify the geometric meaning of the "extra" term cos x sin y in the correct formula.
questions.a: Take x = 30°, y = 60°. sin(30°+60°) = sin 90° = 1. But sin 30° + sin 60° = 1/2 + √3/2 ≈ 1.366 ≠ 1. The "extra" term cos x sin y (and cos y sin x) accounts for the projection of the second angle's sine onto the first angle's cosine direction—geometrically, when rotating by x then y, the vertical component comes from both the sine of the first rotation projected onto the second, and the cosine of the first rotation projected onto the sine of the second. A wrong answer shows the student treats trigonometric functions as linear (additive), missing the rotational composition that creates the cross-terms.

questions.q: Evaluate cos 15° exactly using the cosine difference formula with standard angles. Show all steps including the final simplified radical form.
questions.a: cos 15° = cos(45° - 30°) = cos 45° cos 30° + sin 45° sin 30° = (1/√2)(√3/2) + (1/√2)(1/2) = √3/(2√2) + 1/(2√2) = (√3 + 1)/(2√2). Rationalise: multiply numerator and denominator by √2: = (√6 + √2)/4. A wrong answer like (√3+1)/2√2 without rationalising loses marks in CBSE; writing cos 45° - cos 30° shows the additive misconception; using cos(60°-45°) gives the same result but with different intermediate steps—both are acceptable if correctly executed.

questions.q: Given that sin A = 3/5 and cos B = -12/13, with A in quadrant II and B in quadrant III, determine the quadrant of (A+B) and find the exact value of tan(A+B). Justify your quadrant determination.
questions.a: A in QII ⇒ cos A = -√(1 - 9/25) = -4/5, tan A = -3/4. B in QIII ⇒ sin B = -√(1 - 144/169) = -5/13, tan B = 5/12. tan(A+B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 - tan A tan B) = (-3/4 + 5/12)/(1 - (-3/4)(5/12)) = (-9/12 + 5/12)/(1 + 15/48) = (-4/12)/(63/48) = (-1/3) × (48/63) = -16/63. Since tan(A+B) < 0, (A+B) is in QII or QIV. sin(A+B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B = (3/5)(-12/13) + (-4/5)(-5/13) = -36/65 + 20/65 = -16/65 < 0. cos(A+B) = cos A cos B - sin A sin B = (-4/5)(-12/13) - (3/5)(-5/13) = 48/65 + 15/65 = 63/65 > 0. Thus cos > 0, sin < 0 ⇒ (A+B) in QIV. A wrong quadrant assignment reveals inability to use sign patterns of sine/cosine to locate angles—a frequent board exam error.

questions.q: A student claims: "tan(π/8) can be found by solving the quadratic from tan(π/4) = 2tan(π/8)/(1 - tan²(π/8))". Evaluate this claim: is the equation set up correctly? If yes, solve it and select the correct root with justification. If no, correct the error.
questions.a: The claim is correct. tan(π/4) = 1 = 2t/(1 - t²) where t = tan(π/8). Cross-multiplying: 1 - t² = 2t ⇒ t² + 2t - 1 = 0 ⇒ t = [-2 ± √(4 + 4)]/2 = -1 ± √2. Since π/8 ∈ QI, tan(π/8) > 0, so t = √2 - 1. A wrong answer selecting -1 - √2 ignores the quadrant sign rule; writing t = 1 ± √2 shows algebraic error in quadratic formula; claiming the double-angle formula is tan 2x = 2tan x/(1 + tan²x) confuses it with sin 2x formula.

questions.q: Construct a trigonometric identity of the form sin(x+y)cos(x-y) = ? that simplifies to an expression containing only sin 2x and sin 2y. Prove your identity using sum/difference and double-angle formulas.
questions.a: sin(x+y)cos(x-y) = ½[sin(2x) + sin(2y)]. Proof: sin(x+y)cos(x-y) = ½[sin((x+y)+(x-y)) + sin((x+y)-(x-y))] using 2 sin A cos B = sin(A+B) + sin(A-B) with A=x+y, B=x-y. This gives ½[sin(2x) + sin(2y)]. Alternatively, expand both: (sin x cos y + cos x sin y)(cos x cos y + sin x sin y) = sin x cos x cos²y + sin²x sin y cos y + cos²x sin y cos y + sin x cos x sin²y = sin x cos x(cos²y+sin²y) + sin y cos y(sin²x+cos²x) = sin x cos x + sin y cos y = ½ sin 2x + ½ sin 2y. A poor answer shows inability to combine product-to-sum (node 012) with sum/difference formulas—revealing lack of forward linkage awareness.
